summary: Pilate scourges Jesus; the soldiers plait "a crown of thorns" and a "purple robe" and mock him, "Hail, King of the Jews!" Pilate presents him with "Behold the man!" and repeats, "I find no fault in him," but the charge escalates: "he made himself the Son of God." More afraid, Pilate asks, "Whence art thou?" and receives no answer, then hears that his own authority is only "given thee from above." Cornered by "We have no king but Cæsar," he sits at the Pavement, says "Behold your King!" and delivers him up. Jesus goes "bearing his cross" to Golgotha and is crucified between two others, with Pilate's trilingual title fixed above him and unretracted: "What I have written I have written." The soldiers divide his garments and cast lots for the seamless coat, "that the scripture might be fulfilled." Standing by the cross are his mother and other women; to her he says, "Woman, behold thy son!" and to the beloved disciple, "Behold thy mother!" Knowing "that all things were now accomplished," he says "I thirst," receives vinegar on hyssop, declares "It is finished," and "gave up the ghost." His legs are not broken, but a spear pierces his side and "forthwith came there out blood and water" — scripture fulfilled twice over. Joseph of Arimathaea and Nicodemus bury him with myrrh and aloes in a garden tomb "wherein was never man yet laid."
takeaways: John frames the crucifixion as enthronement: the thorns, the robe, the title in three languages, and the twice-spoken "Behold your King" all say in mockery what the evangelist means in earnest.
"It is finished" is a word of completion rather than exhaustion; the work given him is accomplished, and he then hands over his life rather than having it merely taken.
The unbroken bones and the pierced side are presented as deliberate fulfillments, tying Jesus to the paschal lamb and to the prophetic promise that Israel would look upon the one they pierced.
From the cross Jesus establishes a bond of care between his mother and the disciple, so that even in dying he is forming the household of those who belong to him.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 22:16-18 — they pierced my hands and feet and cast lots for my garments
crossRefs.why: The psalm describes a righteous sufferer surrounded by enemies, his bones exposed and his clothing divided by lot. John quotes it directly at the dividing of the garments, so the whole psalm becomes a script the crucifixion is visibly following.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 53:3-7 — despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, and silent before his accusers
crossRefs.why: Isaiah portrays a servant who is disfigured, bears the iniquity of others, and opens not his mouth. It illuminates both Jesus' silence when Pilate demands "Whence art thou?" and John's insistence that this death is substitutionary and willed, not accidental.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 12:43-46 — the passover lamb, of which no bone shall be broken
crossRefs.why: The law of the passover forbids breaking a bone of the lamb whose blood spares Israel. John notes the hour of preparation, the hyssop that once applied the blood, and the unbroken legs, presenting Jesus as the true paschal lamb dying as the passover lambs are being readied.

crossRefs.label: Zechariah 12:10 — they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and mourn
crossRefs.why: Zechariah promises an outpoured spirit of grace and a people who look on the pierced one and grieve. John cites it at the spear thrust, so the wound becomes not merely proof of death but the object of a repentant, believing gaze.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 3:15 — the woman, her seed, and the promise of a crushed serpent
crossRefs.why: The first promise of deliverance is given to "the woman" and her offspring, not to Eve by name. In the Catholic tradition this is read against Jesus addressing his mother as "Woman" at the cross, seeing the promise reaching its completion at the very moment the serpent's work appears to triumph.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the words "Woman, behold thy son" and "Behold thy mother" are read as more than a dying son arranging his mother's care: because Jesus addresses her by title rather than by name and the disciple is left unnamed, Mary is understood to be given as mother to all who are beloved disciples, which is the scriptural root of Catholic devotion to her as mother of the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the exchange at its plainest level, as a genuine act of filial duty in which Jesus entrusts a widowed mother to a trusted disciple who "took her unto his own home," and they are cautious about extending a specific household arrangement into a universal spiritual relationship. Both traditions honor Mary's fidelity in standing at the cross when almost everyone else had fled, and both see Jesus caring for his own to the very end.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading treats the "blood and water" from the pierced side as a sacramental sign as well as a medical detail, seeing in it the Eucharist and baptism flowing from the opened side of Christ, which is why the Church is described as born from the cross.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take the blood and water first as the eyewitness proof John says it is, "his record is true: and he knoweth that he saith true, that ye might believe," establishing that Jesus was really dead against any suggestion of a swoon. Many also allow a secondary symbolism of cleansing and life, so the traditions differ over emphasis and sacramental weight rather than over the plain claim that a real death has really been witnessed.
